utterances.text: That there's no clear factual basis for that assumption apart from that they did not find anything which is specific on the matter, and therefore it must have been business as usual. That's more or less how I understand this testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just so it's clear, that's obviously not the Prosecution case. The Prosecution case is that these men were doing something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, that's clear. And the witness then clearly on the suggested possibilities said, no, that certainly was not what it was about. You gave him two examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, I don't think he was saying that he knew that it wasn't. I think what he was saying was that type of activity is not what he would consider the normative work or the normative provision, I forget the exact language, "the current normative provisions of an intelligence service." So I was just asking him whether it is possible in his view when he used that phrase did he intend it to mean these other two activities, and I think he's clear that he did not intend it to mean those two other activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at the same time he did not specifically answer your question on what current normative provisions exactly are in in this context, and Mr. Petrovic would oppose against putting such a question to him because it would require him to give an outline of the regulations applicable at that time, but he didn't do that. So to that extent, Mr. Petrovic might be --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just on the basis of one example which we heard in this courtroom, the witness said that as part of their tasks they had the collection of intelligence. This is what Mr. Groome just repeated now. Even that statement of the witness is inconsistent with what he wrote in the report and it is also inconsistent with what are the norms. It is stated in the conclusion that in keeping with the generally accepted standards inherent in internal security services, he could engage persons to co-operate with him in the discharge of his duties. This is a much broader definition than what we have just heard. So intelligence affairs, this is where the dispute arises. This is wherefrom arises the reason to seriously challenge what we have heard here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clear that you would like to cross-examine the witness on these kind of matters, whether that -- whether the Chamber will consider this to be within the framework of what cross-examination in these specific circumstances for this witness would be, we'll have to think about that. Any other matter you would like to raise in cross-examination because we are still exploring why it would take five hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, the second issue would be the document issue, and whether it was possible to insert documents, A; and B, whether in fact this witness has any basis for saying that he has never seen any documents which gave rise to any concern about authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the first question, I almost could answer at that question. That is, that there always is a possibility. And I think that Mr. Groome made a reservation to some extent in one of his questions where he said, of course you can't talk about what happened before you ever started with this job. That is whether in the past anyone would have created or replaced or done anything. Do we expect -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, but then completely nullified that position by asking the question about whether the witness had seen anything that gave cause for concern, which was the basis for my objection to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are apparently two issues here. The one appears to be was there anything in your work which triggered ever the thinking about forgery, et cetera, in whatever way. I think I as broadly as that, put the question to the witness. Now, he clearly said no. It's possible that he didn't look carefully at the documents. Where the documents give a clue for forgeries, then I think that's a reasonable challenge to what he said because even if he told us the truth and he said he never found anything, any information, then it may be because he didn't open his eyes wide enough but he listened carefully enough for any signal which would go to the opposite. That's a perfectly legitimate, I would say perfectly legitimate matter to cross-examine these witnesses on. The other matter is if documents or information do not reveal any indicia of forgery, could they nevertheless have been forgeries which were planted in archives, et cetera? There I would expect that a witness can do a few things, start speculating whether it's possible or not, which doesn't assist. If he would firmly deny that it ever happened, then of course, but in two or three questions you would find the factual basis for such a denial, how could you exclude something if you weren't there 24 hours, 7 days a week. That also seems not to justify many, many hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, it depends what the witness says. I mean, if the witness concedes reasonably, in our submission, that he didn't check the documents very carefully, wasn't looking for forgeries, he doesn't know what happened beforehand and whether there was opportunity for people to put forgeries in, then it would take ten minutes. But if he sticks his heels in the ground and wants to insist on the absolute reliability of his own assessment, well it could take several hours to take him through various documents, take him through the chain of custody, and so on and so forth. I would hope we didn't get to that position, but our Defence involves persuading to a degree, Your Honours, about the lack of authenticity of certain documents, and we would not be content just to leave it as a vague possibility but we would want to demonstrate to Your Honours that it was more than a possibility, it was a probability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Petrovic, you also claim quite some time. Is there anything you would like to add to what Mr. Jordash has said he would like to explore in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, I can only promise that Mr. Jordash and I will be dividing the subjects so that we shall seek to make our respective times devoted to cross as short as possible. Nothing new, nothing different, there is nothing new, nothing different that I can say in the sense that this reduction of time can be significant. Only after having seen all the documents and review them, I will be able to say something more precisely. But when I said three hours before, with all due respect to the Chamber that was my best estimate at the time, but I will be wiser in a couple of days I expect and I promise then to give you my better estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We all hope to grow wiser as age advances, Mr. Petrovic. That's even -- in days we can make progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are two other issues that I would like to touch upon with this witness which may or may not take some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: One is the establishment of the JATD and the establishment of the JSO because, as I indicated I think yesterday, on the face of the report there are pieces of that report which support the Defence position and I'd like to explore that a little. And secondly, I'd like to explore to a degree the chain of reporting and chain of command of the JATD and the -- possibly the JSO, but the focus will be on the JATD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what would the witness -- at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, the witness gives -- sorry, the commission report deals with the way in which the minister would set up -- it would be the minister who would set up a special unit and the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, from what I understand from the report they say, if anyone it's set up that, it may well have been the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's also not very firm.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, but I would want to explore whether the witness's answers or the commission's conclusions arose from their understanding of how things were normally done, which is our Defence case, that such a unit would have to be set up by the minister. And secondly, as it is in the report, that once the unit was set up, there was a degree of missing out of certain chains in the chain of command, i.e., the chief of the service, and the unit itself would or could bypass the chief and go straight to the minister in terms of certain functions and certain functioning of the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I understand. I was just exploring -- I'm not taking over, it's for you to cross-examine the witness, but I was exploring what the issues were and come to a reasonable estimate of the time needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I did say three to four. My guess is that's excessive but I wanted to leave myself some room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- have some reserve time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's, for scheduling purposes, the Chamber is not very fond of because if you claim more time, you use more time, that's the general practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just mindful of giving estimates and going over them which we've been guilty of in the past, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, slowly moving to a solution, but I'd like to move now from these witnesses to witness JF-039. Mr. Groome, how much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have the estimate at hand, but I think the estimate that we gave in November 2000, I was three hours, and I believe -- I mean, hope -- I always hope, I always try to do it shorter, but I wouldn't want to commit to anything less than three hours with that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, Defence, perhaps having a better and also keeping in mind the way in which I just explained how we analyse what is needed for cross-examination of witnesses, that is a clear view of what do we want to establish through this witness and not what subjects could we explore in order to find out that the witness can't tell us anything about that because that's unlimited. So we have to find a fair balance between fishing expeditions and a very focused clear cross examination. For JF-039, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I should say that this witness gives -- or purports to give chapter and verse and places Mr. Stanisic in control of almost all the Serbian events in the Krajina in 1991, so I couldn't imagine cross-examining him for less than three and probably closer to four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Jordash was in a better situation to make his estimates because I finished with Maksic yesterday and last night and I focused on that. Over the night and this morning I tried to take a look at the testimony of this witness. I believe that he directly involves our client in a number of situations, and my best estimate is that we should be requiring between two and a half and three hours for this witness. But as my colleague Petrovic has said and as Mr. Jordash has said, I am trying to reserve some time, but if I manage to follow your instructions and focus only on the essentials, of course that time can be that much shorter. Thank you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has reached a conclusion as to how to proceed. The Chamber wishes to start on Wednesday -- on Monday with the examination-in-chief of witness JF-039 and expects you, Mr. Groome, to do your utmost best to finish the examination-in-chief in the first two sessions of that day. Then we'll continue with the cross-examination of witness JF-039. It may well be that we are in a better position to give further estimates on how much time we would need by the end of the Monday session. Meanwhile, we'll see whether it's possible for witnesses JF-094 and 095 to be prepared to travel, if need be, on Tuesday, that is the Tuesday where we'll continue the cross-examination of witness JF-039. But by Monday the end of the day we'll be better able to assess whether we would need a Wednesday session still for conclusion of the cross-examination of witness JF-039 or whether we'd have Wednesday available, because the Chamber considers that the cross-examination of witnesses JF-094 and 095 would take close to a day at least, that that would be a reasonable projection of the time we would need, that is anything between in total three, three and a half hours. We'll see how it develops, as we always do, but for the time being, the schedule would be let's get started with JF-039, let's immediately then continue with his cross-examination, and let's see whether there's any time left in that week on Wednesday for recalling witnesses JF-094 and 095 to be cross-examined. If that's not possible, they will be called to be cross-examined later. This is the suggestion by the Chamber at this moment. The hearing on Wednesday is still a bit uncertain because it requires a lot of reshuffling. So whether that would be morning or afternoon is still to be considered, and whether it's at all possible because we need the co-operation of other Chambers for the reshuffling exercise. Any comments on this suggested way to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it has been stated that this is a suggestion from Their Honours and this gave me the liberty to stand up and say the following: If this is a suggestion, I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to reconsider, and if you allow me to, I'll give you my suggestion. JF-039 has only been announced as a witness yesterday or the day before yesterday and since I was examining the witness who was testifying at the time, I learned about that witness yesterday. I have four days to contact possible individuals who know him and to prepare. My learned friend Mr. Petrovic wanted to ask this, as did I, we believed that the two commission witnesses would have their cross-examination next week and we hoped that within that schedule my cross would have taken place on the 20th. I can prepare myself by Wednesday; however, it is highly unrealistic for me to be able to prepare myself for Monday. I really apologise. However, one of the commission witnesses said that he was available on Monday. Why not start with him instead and conduct his cross-examination at the end of which we could see how we stand. This would help me gain some time. As I said, despite all the shortcoming these commission witnesses have been announced and we have known about them for months, whereas JF-039 has only been put on our notice yesterday, and it is really not enough time for me to prepare for his cross-examination by Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One the problems of your solution is that only one of the commission witnesses is available on Monday, the other is not. So we can't -- the other one unless he has meanwhile explored the possibility to come back on Wednesday. We'll explore that possibility. We have to balance quite many problems, that's the vulnerability of witness JF-039, availability of the commission witnesses. I see since you have now a preference to first conclude the cross-examination of the commission witnesses, suddenly all the problems in asking for a delay, now you say, well, we have prepared for that since six months. You see how quickly situations and positions can change. We'll certainly consider that and we'll also try to find out whether it would be possible at all to hear both commission witnesses, their testimony in cross-examination on Monday, if not then we are facing there a problem as well. And I said we have to -- we have to finish today, unfortunately, apart from that we are running out of tapes. It's a bit of a hectic and chaotic way we are proceeding at this moment. As I said before, you'll soon receive an invitation to further discuss how to avoid chaos and hectic situations, and I hope that we'll be able to inform you today. We might need first to consult with VWS as to the possibilities of flexible filling in Monday, Tuesday for witness JF-095, we'll inform you as soon as possible. Tomorrow is unfortunately a UN who holiday, but I take it that you can be reached if need be.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, I understood him to say that he had some obligations he had to attend to, but he did not exclude the possibility that he might appear on Monday. So could the possibility for him to appear with the other witness on Monday please be explored.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I invited him to explore his possibilities. We will we will adjourn. First we turn into open session again. If we open one curtain, then that make it public enough.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.
